claim: Microbial communities routinely have several possible species compositions or community states observed for the same environmental parameters.
source: Microbial communities routinely have several possible species compositions or community states observed for the same environmental parameters.
evidence: This is a statement about observed patterns in microbial communities, supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Changes in environmental parameters can trigger abrupt and persistent transitions (regime shifts) between community states.
source: Changes in these parameters can trigger abrupt and persistent transitions (regime shifts) between such community states.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to ecosystem regime shifts literature.

claim: Multistability requires microbial species to have different stoichiometries of essential nutrients.
source: Our results suggest that multistability requires microbial species to have different stoichiometries of essential nutrients.
evidence: This is a main finding from the model presented in the manuscript, supported by numerical simulations and mathematical arguments.

claim: Balanced nutrient supply promotes multistability and species diversity.
source: We also find that a balanced nutrient supply promotes multistability and species diversity, yet make individual community states less stable.
evidence: This finding is demonstrated through model simulations shown in Figures 3B and 4A.

claim: Balanced nutrient supply makes individual community states less stable.
source: We also find that a balanced nutrient supply promotes multistability and species diversity, yet make individual community states less stable.
evidence: This is demonstrated through analysis of feasible ranges shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Recent metagenomics studies revealed that microbial communities living in similar environments are often composed of rather different sets of species.
source: Recent metagenomics studies revealed that microbial communities living in similar environments are often composed of rather different sets of species (Zhou et al., 2007; Lahti et al., 2014; Lozupone et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2013; Pagaling et al., 2017; Gonze et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to metagenomics studies.

claim: Regime shifts significantly alter the function of a microbial community and are difficult to reverse.
source: Such transitions, known as ecosystem regime shifts, significantly alter the function of a microbial community and are difficult to reverse.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of regime shifts, supported by ecosystem literature.

claim: The majority of modeling approaches explicitly taking nutrients into account are based on the classic MacArthur consumer-resource model and its variants.
source: The majority of modeling approaches explicitly taking nutrients into account are based on the classic MacArthur consumer-resource model and its variants (MacArthur and Levins, 1964; MacArthur, 1970; Huisman and Weissing, 1999; Tikhonov and Monasson, 2017; Posfai et al., 2017; Goldford et al., 2018; Goyal et al., 2018; Butler and O'Dwyer, 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling literature, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The MacArthur consumer-resource model assumes that every species co-utilizes several substitutable nutrients of a single type.
source: This model assumes that every species co-utilizes several substitutable nutrients of a single type (e.g. carbon sources).
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the MacArthur model, based on established knowledge of this model.

claim: Nutrients required for growth of a species exist in the form of several essential (non-substitutable) types including sources of C, N, P, Fe, etc.
source: However, nutrients required for growth of a species exist in the form of several essential (non-substitutable) types including sources of C, N, P, Fe, etc.
evidence: This is a statement about biological reality, based on established knowledge of microbial nutrition.

claim: Real ecosystems driven by competition for multiple essential nutrients have been extensively experimentally studied.
source: Real ecosystems driven by competition for multiple essential nutrients have been extensively experimentally studied (see recent papers; Fanin et al., 2015; Browning et al., 2017; Camenzind et al., 2018 and references therein).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The theoretical foundation for all existing consumer-resource models capturing growth on multiple essential nutrients has been laid in Tilman (1982).
source: The theoretical foundation for all existing consumer-resource models capturing this type of growth has been laid in Tilman (1982), where a model with two essential resources has been introduced and studied.
evidence: This is a statement about the history of theoretical ecology, supported by citation.

claim: Models with three or more essential resources have been shown to sometimes result in oscillations and chaos.
source: Future studies extended Tilman's approach to three and more essential resources, where it has been shown to sometimes result in oscillations and chaos (Huisman and Weissing, 1999; Huisman and Weissing, 2001; Shoresh et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing oscillations and chaos.

claim: All previously studied models accounted for just a single metabolite per each essential nutrient.
source: However, all the previously studied models accounted for just a single metabolite per each essential nutrient.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of previous models, based on review of the literature.

claim: The model has a very large number of possible steady states classified by their distinct species compositions.
source: We show that our model has a very large number of possible steady states classified by their distinct species compositions.
evidence: This is a finding from the model analysis, demonstrated through enumeration of states.

claim: Game-theoretical methods adapted from the stable marriage problem can predict all steady states based only on the ranked lists of competitive abilities of individual species for each of the nutrients.
source: Using game-theoretical methods adapted from the well-known stable marriage (or stable matching) problem (Gale and Shapley, 1962; Gusfield and Irving, 1989), we predict all these states based only on the ranked lists of competitive abilities of individual species for each of the nutrients.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the approach used in the study, supported by mathematical derivation in the appendix.

claim: For a given set of nutrient supply rates, more than one state could be simultaneously feasible, thereby allowing for multistability.
source: We further demonstrate that for a given set of nutrient supply rates, more than one state could be simultaneously feasible, thereby allowing for multistability.
evidence: This is demonstrated through Monte Carlo sampling of nutrient supply rates shown in Figure 3.

claim: The overall number of stable states in the model is exponentially large.
source: While the overall number of stable states in our model is exponentially large, only very few of them can be realized for a given set of environmental conditions defined by nutrient supply rates.
evidence: This is inferred from the enumeration of states in the 6C × 6N × 36S model.

claim: Only very few stable states can be realized for a given set of environmental conditions defined by nutrient supply rates.
source: While the overall number of stable states in our model is exponentially large, only very few of them can be realized for a given set of environmental conditions defined by nutrient supply rates.
evidence: This is shown through Monte Carlo sampling in Figure 3A.

claim: The principal component analysis of predicted microbial abundances shows a separation between the alternative stable states reminiscent of real-life microbial ecosystems.
source: The principal component analysis of predicted microbial abundances in our model shows a separation between the alternative stable states reminiscent of real-life microbial ecosystems.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each species always has exactly one growth-limiting resource and one non-limiting resource.
source: Thus, each species always has exactly one growth-limiting resource and one non-limiting resource.
evidence: This follows from Liebig's law of the minimum as applied in the model.

claim: The number of species present in a steady state of any consumer-resource model cannot exceed K + M − the total number of nutrients.
source: One of the universal consequences of this principle is that the number of species present in a steady state of any consumer-resource model cannot exceed K + M − the total number of nutrients.
evidence: This is a consequence of the competitive exclusion principle applied to consumer-resource models.

claim: There is a one-to-one correspondence between the model system and a variant of the stable matching problem in game theory.
source: We greatly simplified the task of finding all steady states in our model by the discovery of the exact correspondence between our system and a variant of the celebrated stable matching (or stable marriage) problem in game theory and economics (Gale and Shapley, 1962; Gusfield and Irving, 1989).
evidence: This is a methodological finding, demonstrated in Appendix 3.

claim: States with larger feasible volumes generally tend to be more resilient with respect to fluctuations in nutrient supply.
source: States with larger feasible volumes generally tend to be more resilient with respect to fluctuations in nutrient supply.
evidence: This is based on the concept of structural stability from previous literature.

claim: In general, one type of stability does not imply another.
source: Note, that in general, one type of stability does not imply another.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the classification of states in Figure 1F.

claim: Out of 34 possible steady states in the 2C × 2N × 4S model, there are only seven uninvadable ones.
source: Out of 34 possible steady states realized for different ranges of nutrient supply rates there are only seven uninvadable ones.
evidence: This is a result from enumeration of states in the 2C × 2N × 4S model.

claim: In the 2C × 2N × 4S model, only one of the states turned out to be dynamically unstable.
source: In the 2C × 2N × 4S model only one of the states (labelled seven in Figure 1B) turned out to be dynamically unstable, while for the remaining 33 states small perturbations of microbial abundances present in the state do not trigger a change of the state.
evidence: This is a result from dynamic stability analysis of the 2C × 2N × 4S model.

claim: Normalized feasible ranges of uninvadable states have a broad log-normal distribution.
source: In general we find that normalized feasible ranges of uninvadable states in our model have a broad log-normal distribution (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for details).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 through Monte Carlo sampling.

claim: Uninvadable and dynamically stable states correspond to natural endpoints of the microbial community assembly process.
source: Indeed, such states correspond to natural endpoints of the microbial community assembly process.
evidence: This is an inference about the biological meaning of these states.

claim: Uninvadable and dynamically stable states would persist for as long as the nutrient supply rates do not change outside of their structural stability range.
source: They would persist for as long as the nutrient supply rates do not change outside of their structural stability range.
evidence: This follows from the definitions of structural stability and dynamic stability.

claim: Whenever feasible ranges of two or more states overlap, multistability ensues.
source: Whenever feasible ranges of two or more states overlap (see Figure 2B) - multistability ensues.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the definition of multistability.

claim: The states in the overlapping region of their feasibility ranges constitute true alternative stable states.
source: Note that the states in the overlapping region of their feasibility ranges constitute true alternative stable states defined and studied in the ecosystems literature (Sutherland, 1974; Holling, 1973; May, 1977; Fukami and Nakajima, 2011; Bush et al., 2017).
evidence: This connects the model results to established concepts in ecology literature.

claim: The existence of alternative stable states goes hand-in-hand with regime shifts manifesting themselves as large discontinuous and hysteretic changes of species abundances.
source: The existence of alternative stable states goes hand-in-hand with regime shifts manifesting themselves as large discontinuous and hysteretic changes of species abundances (Scheffer and Carpenter, 2003).
evidence: This is based on established theory of regime shifts, supported by citation.

claim: When feasible ranges of a pair of states do not overlap but share a boundary, the transition between these states is smooth and non-hysteretic.
source: Conversely, when feasible ranges of a pair of states do not overlap with each other but share a boundary (Figure 2A), the transition between these states is smooth and non-hysteretic (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Dynamically unstable states always accompany multistable regions in the model.
source: As expected for regime shifts, dynamically unstable states always accompany multistable regions in our model (Scheffer and Carpenter, 2003) (see below for a detailed discussion of the interplay between multistability and dynamically unstable states).
evidence: This is observed in the model and consistent with regime shift theory.

claim: Regime shifts are possible only for nine pairs of uninvadable states in the 2C × 2N × 4S model.
source: One can see that regime shifts are possible only for of nine pairs of uninvadable states.
evidence: This is determined by systematic analysis of overlapping feasible ranges shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All regime shifts in the 2C × 2N × 4S model are driven by the same bistable switch in which two pairs of species compete and mutually exclude each other.
source: This is because all regime shifts are driven by the same bistable switch in which these pairs of species compete and mutually exclude each other.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of the regime shift network.

claim: The dynamically unstable state #7 is formed by the union of all four keystone species.
source: The dynamically unstable state #7 is formed by the union of all four keystone species and, when perturbed, collapses into a state with either one or another keystone set.
evidence: This is observed from the composition of state #7 and its dynamic behavior.

claim: States connected by a continuous transition share the same pair of keystone species.
source: Conversely, states connected by a continuous transition share the same pair of keystone species.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of continuous transitions in the model.

claim: There are 8633 regime shifts between 893 uninvadable dynamically stable states in the 6C × 6N × 36S model.
source: Figure 2F shows a much larger network of 8633 regime shifts between 893 uninvadable dynamically stable states in the 6C × 6N × 36S realization of our model.
evidence: This is a result from systematic enumeration in the larger model.

claim: The network modularity analysis revealed seven network modules in the 6C × 6N × 36S model.
source: The network modularity analysis (see Materials and methods for details) revealed seven network modules indicating that pairs of states that could possibly undergo a regime shift are clustered together in the multi-dimensional space of nutrient supply rates.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F using network analysis methods.

claim: The modular structure suggests the existence of distinct sets of keystone species driving regime shifts within each module.
source: This modular structure suggests the existence of distinct sets of keystone species driving regime shifts within each module.
evidence: This is an inference from the network modularity structure.

claim: For some supply rates up to five stable states can be simultaneously feasible.
source: Note that for some supply rates up to five stable states can be simultaneously feasible.
evidence: This is observed in Monte Carlo sampling shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The probability to encounter cases with five stable states is exponentially small.
source: However, the probability to encounter such cases is exponentially small.
evidence: This is shown by the distribution in Figure 3A.

claim: Multistability in the model is only possible if individual microbial species have different C:N stoichiometry.
source: Like in a simple special case of regime shift between two microbial species studied in Tilman (1982), multistability in our model is only possible if individual microbial species have different C:N stoichiometry.
evidence: This is demonstrated through numerical simulations and mathematical arguments in Appendix 5.

claim: When all species have the same stoichiometry, for every set of nutrient supply rates the community has a unique uninvadable state, and all these states are dynamically stable.
source: That is to say, in this case for every set of nutrient supply rates the community has a unique uninvadable state, and all these states are dynamically stable.
evidence: This follows from the analysis in Appendix 5.

claim: The likelihood of multistability has a sharp peak around the well-balanced C:N nutrient supply rates.
source: Figure 3B shows this to be the case: the likelihood of multistability has a sharp peak around the well-balanced C:N nutrient supply rates.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B through Monte Carlo sampling.

claim: In the region of balanced nutrient supply, multiple stable states are present for roughly 15% of nutrient supply rate combinations.
source: In this region multiple stable states are present for roughly 15% of nutrient supply rate combinations.
evidence: This is quantified from the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The highest chance to observe multistability will be when the ratio of nutrient supply rates is close to the average C:N stoichiometry of species in the community.
source: Hence, in general, we predict that the highest chance to observe multistability will be when the ratio of nutrient supply rates is close to the average C:N stoichiometry of species in the community.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the PCA plot, five distinct clusters are observed, each corresponding to a single dynamically stable uninvadable state.
source: One can see five distinct clusters, each corresponding to a single dynamically stable uninvadable state.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: All states are aligned along a quasi-1D manifold with an alternating order of stable and unstable states.
source: Furthermore, all states are aligned along a quasi-1D manifold with an alternating order of stable and unstable states.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The gaps between neighboring clusters in PCA plots would correspond to dynamically unstable states of the ecosystem.
source: If this is the case, the gaps between neighboring clusters would correspond to dynamically unstable states of the ecosystem, which may be experimentally observable as long transients in community composition.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the PCA results.

claim: A balanced supply of nutrients promotes species diversity.
source: Interestingly, a balanced supply of nutrients also promotes species diversity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The species richness is the largest (around 10.5) for balanced nutrient supply rates in the 6C × 6N × 36S model.
source: The species richness is the largest (around 10.5) for balanced nutrient supply rates, while dropping down to the absolute minimal value of six in two extreme cases of very large imbalance of supply rates, where the nutrient supplied in excess becomes irrelevant in competition.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The number of distinct community states has a sharp peak at balanced nutrient supply.
source: The number of distinct community states also has a sharp peak at balanced nutrient supply (see 3-orders of magnitude difference in Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: For balanced nutrient supply rates, the relationship between species' competitiveness and its prevalence in the community is much less pronounced than for imbalanced ones.
source: For balanced nutrient supply rates the relationship between species' competitiveness and its prevalence in the community is much less pronounced than for imbalanced ones.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All 36 species in the pool are present in some of the environments.
source: Note that all 36 species in our pool are present in some of the environments.
evidence: This is observed from the prevalence analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: More competitive species tend to survive in a larger subset of environments.
source: In general, more competitive species tend to survive in a larger subset of environments (see the dashed curve in Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown by the trend line in Figure 4B.

claim: Some of the least competitive species survive in a broad range of environments.
source: However, we also find that some of the least competitive species (those at the right end of the x-axis in Figure 4B) survive in a broad range of environments.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There is an exponential increase of the number of uninvadable states as a function of species richness.
source: Figure 4C shows an exponential increase of the number of uninvadable states as a function of species richness.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: All uninvadable states with less than 10 species are dynamically stable in the 6C × 6N × 36S model.
source: In our 6C × 6N × 36S model all uninvadable states with less than 10 species are dynamically stable (solid line in Figure 4C), while those with 10 or more species can be both stable or unstable (dashed line in Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The fraction of stable states to dynamically unstable ones decreases with species richness.
source: Overall, the fraction of stable states to dynamically unstable ones decreases with species richness.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The probability for a state to be dynamically unstable increases with the number of species.
source: In other words, the probability for a state to be dynamically unstable increases with the number of species.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 4C.

claim: The model behaves similar to the gLV model in Robert May's study regarding the relationship between diversity and stability.
source: In this aspect, our model behaves similar to the gLV model in Robert May's study (May, 1972).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work based on similar trends.

claim: There is a negative correlation between the species richness of a stable state and its feasible range of nutrient supplies.
source: In Figure 4D, we show a negative correlation between the species richness of a stable state and its feasible range of nutrient supplies.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The number of species in an ecosystem has detrimental effect on the structural stability of the community.
source: Thus in our model the number of species in an ecosystem has detrimental effect on the structural stability of the community quantifying its robustness to fluctuating nutrient supply (Rohr et al., 2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and relates to previous work on structural stability.

claim: The empirically observed exponential decay of state's feasible range with its number of species is well described by a two-fold decrease per each species added.
source: The empirically observed exponential decay of state's feasible range with its number of species is well described by a two-fold decrease per each species added (see Serván et al., 2018 and Grilli et al., 2017 for related results in the gLV model).
evidence: This is observed from the data in Figure 4D and compared to previous work.

claim: In well-balanced environments, a large number of states are carving all possible combinations of nutrient supply into many small and overlapping ranges.
source: Thus, in well-balanced environments a large number of states are carving all possible combinations of nutrient supply into many small and overlapping ranges.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: In nutrient-balanced environments, we expect to observe a high diversity of species in the existing communities.
source: In nutrient-balanced environments, we expect to observe a high diversity of species in the existing communities.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Species in balanced environments can form a very large number of possible combinations (uninvadable states).
source: These species can form a very large number of possible combinations (uninvadable states).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each community state in balanced environments could be realized only for a narrow range of nutrient supply rates indicating their low structural stability.
source: Each of these states could be realized only for a narrow range of nutrient supply rates indicating their low structural stability.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In environments with highly variable nutrient supplies, the community will frequently shift between states.
source: In environments with highly variable nutrient supplies the community will frequently shift between these states.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the low structural stability of states in balanced environments.

claim: Many of the steady states in the balanced regime are dynamically unstable giving rise to multistability and regime shifts.
source: Furthermore, many of the steady states in this regime are dynamically unstable giving rise to multistability and regime shifts.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3B and 4C.

claim: Microbial communities growing on an imbalanced mix of essential nutrients have relatively low diversity.
source: Conversely, microbial communities growing on an imbalanced mix of essential nutrients have relatively low diversity (Figure 4A) but are characterized by a high degree of structural and dynamic stability (see Figure 4D and Figure 4C respectively).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 4A, 4C, and 4D.

claim: The model is the first consumer-resource model capable of multistability between several states, each characterized by a high diversity of species.
source: To the best of our knowledge our model is the first consumer-resource model capable of multistability between several states, each characterized by a high diversity of species.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model based on review of the literature.

claim: The model extends Tilman's scenario to the case of multiple nutrients of each type.
source: We extend Tilman's scenario (Tilman, 1982) in which the growth of two species is limited by a pair of essential resources to the case of multiple nutrients of each type.
evidence: This describes the relationship of the current model to previous work.

claim: Common variants of the MacArthur model assume identical biomass yields of different species growing on a given nutrient.
source: Common variants of the MacArthur model assume identical biomass yields of different species growing on a given nutrient (Tikhonov and Monasson, 2017; Posfai et al., 2017; Goldford et al., 2018; Goyal et al., 2018; Butler and O'Dwyer, 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about common assumptions in MacArthur model variants, supported by citations.

claim: In the MacArthur model with identical yields, the absence of multistability is guaranteed by a convex Lyapunov function.
source: In this case, the absence of multistability is guaranteed by a convex Lyapunov function (MacArthur, 1970) guiding any dynamical trajectory of the system to its unique minimum.
evidence: This is a statement about the mathematical properties of the MacArthur model, supported by citation.

claim: A MacArthur model with different nutrient yields of different species is capable of multistability.
source: However, a MacArthur model with different nutrient yields of different species is capable of multistability.
evidence: This is an inference about the MacArthur model based on the role of yield variation.

claim: Another type of growth function with two essential resources has been shown to have bistable solutions even for identical species stoichiometries.
source: Another type of growth function with two essential resources has been shown to have bistable solutions even for identical species stoichiometries (see Figure 5C in Marsland et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The larger the variation of C:N ratio of individual microbes, the higher is the likelihood to observe multistability.
source: Given that multistability in our model is impossible in communities of species with identical stoichiometries, it is reasonable to expect that the larger is the variation of C:N ratio of individual microbes, the higher is the likelihood to observe multistability.
evidence: This is investigated in Figure 5 through systematic variation of yield parameters.

claim: The likelihood of finding nutrient supply rates with multistability systematically decreases with standard deviation of the logarithm of species stoichiometry.
source: It shows that the likelihood of finding nutrient supply rates with multistability systematically decreases with standard deviation of the logarithm of species stoichiometry.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: About half of the combinations of species stoichiometries yielded no multistable states at all.
source: We also found that about half of the combinations of species stoichiometries yielded no multistable states at all.
evidence: This is observed from the simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: Nutrient stoichiometry of phytoplankton species in marine ecosystems is relatively universal with C:N:P ≃ 106:16:1 known as Redfield ratio.
source: Nutrient stoichiometry of phytoplankton species in marine ecosystems has been known to be relatively universal with C:N:P ≃ 106:16:1 known as Redfield ratio (Redfield, 1958).
evidence: This is established knowledge about phytoplankton stoichiometry, supported by citation.

claim: Species-to-species variability of C:N ratio for phytoplankton is rather small with logarithmic standard deviation estimated to be around 0.05.
source: Thus species-to-species variability of C:N ratio for phytoplankton is rather small with logarithmic standard deviation estimated to be around 0.05 based on data from Finkel et al. (2016).
evidence: This is based on data from cited study.

claim: For phytoplankton, multistability in the model is rather unlikely (observed in ∼3% of nutrient supply combinations).
source: In this limit, the multistability in our model is rather unlikely (observed in ∼3% of nutrient supply combinations, see green arrow in Figure 5).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model applied to phytoplankton stoichiometry data.

claim: The likelihood of multistability is low (∼1%) for the mammalian gut microbiome.
source: The likelihood of multistability is also low (∼1%) for the mammalian gut microbiome, where variability of the logarithm of C:N ratio in different 'keystone' gut species studied in Reese et al. (2018) is around 0.03.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model applied to gut microbiome stoichiometry data.

claim: Significant deviations from the Redfield ratio have been reported in terrestrial ecosystems such as soil.
source: The chances of multistability increase in terrestrial ecosystems such as soil, where significant deviations from the Redfield ratio have been reported (Cleveland and Liptzin, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: For grassland leaf litter community, the likelihood of multistability is predicted to be around 10%.
source: For example, using the data for the microbial species from grassland leaf litter community reported in Mouginot et al. (2014), with log(C:N) variability of 0.12 we predict the likelihood of multistability to be around 10%.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the model applied to soil microbiome stoichiometry data.

claim: When nutrient supplies are balanced, microbial community multistability is relatively common.
source: When nutrient supplies are balanced, microbial community multistability is relatively common.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For balanced nutrients, the community can be in one of many different states, characterized by different combinations of limiting nutrients.
source: Furthermore, for balanced nutrients the community can be in one of many different states, characterized by different combinations of limiting nutrients.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: States in balanced environments tend to have high species diversity.
source: These states tend to have high species diversity (Figure 4A) – a trend consistent with lake ecosystems in Interlandi and Kilham (2001) – and relatively small range of feasible supply rates (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and consistent with cited experimental work.

claim: States in balanced environments have relatively small range of feasible supply rates.
source: These states tend to have high species diversity (Figure 4A) – a trend consistent with lake ecosystems in Interlandi and Kilham (2001) – and relatively small range of feasible supply rates (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Regime shifts can be easily triggered by changes in nutrient supply in balanced environments.
source: Hence, regime shifts can be easily triggered by changes in nutrient supply.
evidence: This is inferred from the small feasible ranges shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The balanced region is characterized by a complex relationship between species competitiveness and survival.
source: The balanced region is characterized by a complex relationship between species competitiveness and survival, so that even relatively poor competitors could occasionally have high prevalence (species in the upper right corner of Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When nitrogen supply greatly exceeds carbon supply, the community has a unique uninvadable state.
source: In the opposite limit, the supply of nutrients of one type (say nitrogen) greatly exceeds that of another type (say carbon). For such imbalanced supply, the community has a unique uninvadable state, where every carbon nutrient supports the growth of the single most competitive species.
evidence: This is inferred from the model behavior in the imbalanced regime.

claim: For imbalanced supply, nitrogen nutrients are not limiting the growth of any species and thus have no impact on species survival and community diversity.
source: Nitrogen nutrients are not limiting the growth of any species and thus have no impact on species survival and community diversity.
evidence: This follows from Liebig's law as applied in the model.

claim: The average diversity of microbial communities in nutrient-imbalanced environments is low (about one half of that for balanced supply conditions).
source: As a consequence, the average diversity of microbial communities in such nutrient-imbalanced environments is low (about one half of that for balanced supply conditions).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Addition of high quantities of one essential nutrient tends to decrease species diversity.
source: This is in agreement with many experimental studies showing that addition of high quantities of one essential nutrient (e.g. as nitrogen fertilizer) tends to decrease species diversity. This has been reported in numerous experimental studies cited in the chapter 'Resource richness and species diversity' of Tilman (1982) as well as in recent experiments in microbial communities (Mello et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The rank order of competitive abilities fully defines the total number of stable states and their invadability.
source: As we showed above, the rank order of the former fully defines the total number of stable states and their invadability.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the stable matching approach.

claim: Multistability highly depends on combination of species' nutrient yields.
source: On the other hand, multistability highly depends on combination of species' nutrient yields.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: A tradeoff between competitive abilities for different nutrients may exist due to a limited amount of internal resources a species can allocate for consumption of all nutrients.
source: Such tradeoff may exist due to a limited amount of internal resources (such as the overall number of transporters) this species can allocate for consumption of all nutrients.
evidence: This is a biological explanation for potential tradeoffs.

claim: A tradeoff between competitive abilities for different nutrients was shown to result in increased species diversity in well-balanced environments, but does not lead to multistability.
source: This type of tradeoff was shown to result in an increased species diversity in well-balanced environments, but does not lead to multistability (Posfai et al., 2017; Tikhonov, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Negative correlations between competitive abilities for different nutrients are expected to increase the total number of stable states.
source: Negative correlations between species' competitive abilities for carbon and nitrogen are expected to increase the total number of stable states in our model, while positive correlations - to decrease it.
evidence: This is a prediction based on analogy to previous work on the stable marriage problem.

claim: Growth-yield tradeoff states that microbial species with faster growth on a given nutrient tend to use it less efficiently.
source: It is known as a 'growth-yield tradeoff', which states that microbial species with faster growth on a given nutrient tend to use it less efficiently (have a smaller yield) (Pfeiffer et al., 2001; Beardmore et al., 2011; Novak et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about microbial physiology, supported by citations.

claim: Growth-yield tradeoff is expected to increase the likelihood of multistability in the model.
source: Growth-yield tradeoff is expected to increase the likelihood of multistability in our model.
evidence: This is a prediction based on analysis of the model with this tradeoff.

claim: In Tilman's model, if the species with the higher growth rate on carbon has a smaller yield on this resource than the other species, bistability always ensues.
source: It could be demonstrated already in the model of Tilman (1982) with two species competing for two essential resources. If the species with the higher growth rate on, say, carbon source has a smaller yield on this resource than the other species - bistability always ensues.
evidence: This is a statement about the behavior of Tilman's model, based on analysis.

claim: Multistability is expected to be more common in microbial ecosystems than in macroscopic ecosystems due to the growth-yield tradeoff.
source: Conversely, multistability is expected to be more common in microbial ecosystems due to the growth-yield tradeoff.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the difference in tradeoffs between microbial and macroscopic ecosystems.

claim: The three types of stability are largely independent from each other.
source: First, as evident from Figure 1F, the three types of stability are largely independent from each other.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Communities growing on a well balanced mix of nutrients tend to have high species diversity.
source: Second, communities growing on a well balanced mix of nutrients tend to have high species diversity (see peak in Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The similar effect of balanced nutrients promoting diversity was demonstrated in other consumer resource models.
source: The similar effect was demonstrated in other consumer resource models (Posfai et al., 2017; Tikhonov and Monasson, 2017; Taillefumier et al., 2017; Marsland et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The model follows the general trend reported in May (1972) regarding diversity and stability.
source: In this sense our model follows the general trend reported in May (1972).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous work on diversity-stability relationships.

claim: The existence of dynamically unstable states always goes hand in hand with multistability.
source: The existence of dynamically unstable states always goes hand in hand with multistability (Scheffer and Carpenter, 2003) (see the dashed line in Figure 2D for an illustration of this effect in our model).
evidence: This is supported by citation and demonstrated in Figure 2D.

claim: The model can be extended to accommodate generalist species capable of using more than one nutrient of each type.
source: First, one could include generalist species capable of using more than one nutrient of each type.
evidence: This is a proposed extension of the model.

claim: Many of the results of the current study would be extendable to a model with diauxic shifts.
source: Since at any state each of the species is using a 'specialist strategy', that is to say, it is growing on a single carbon and a single nitrogen source, we expect that many of the results of the current study would be extendable to this model.
evidence: This is a prediction about the generalizability of the results.

claim: The stable marriage problem can be used to predict the stable states of microbial communities with diauxic shifts.
source: Interestingly, the stable marriage problem can be used to predict the stable states of microbial communities with diauxic shifts between substitutable resources (Goyal et al., 2018) and those in communities growing on a mix of two essential nutrients as in this study.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It is straightforward to generalize the model to Monod's growth equation and to take into account non-zero death rate.
source: It is straightforward to generalize our model to Monod's growth equation and to take into account non-zero death rate (or maintenance cost) of individual species (see Appendix 1).
evidence: This is stated as a straightforward extension, detailed in Appendix 1.

claim: The model can be extended to include cross-feeding between species.
source: One can extend our model to include cross-feeding between the species.
evidence: This is a proposed extension of the model.

claim: Including cross-feeding would allow the number of species to exceed the number of externally supplied resources.
source: These byproducts should be counted among nutrient sources and thus would allow the number of species to exceed the number of externally supplied resources.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of including cross-feeding.

claim: Densely interconnected networks of regime shifts can be viewed as maps guiding the selection of the optimal environmental trajectory leading to the desired stable species composition.
source: Thus, densely interconnected networks of regime shifts shown in Figure 2E–F can be viewed as maps guiding the selection of the optimal environmental trajectory leading to the desired stable species composition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the practical utility of the regime shift networks.

claim: Microbial ecosystems described by the model might have a relatively small number of key drivers of regime shifts roughly corresponding to network modules.
source: These maps also suggest that microbial ecosystems described by our model might have a relatively small number of key drivers of regime shifts roughly corresponding to network modules (see Figure 2F).
evidence: This is inferred from the network modularity analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Regime shifts in each module are driven by the competition between two mutually exclusive sets of keystone species.
source: Regime shifts in each of the modules are driven by the competition between two mutually exclusive sets of keystone species.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of regime shifts in the 2C × 2N × 4S model.

claim: In addition to keystone species, states also include 'satellite' species that do not generally affect the bistable switch.
source: In addition to these keystone species, states also include 'satellite' species that do not generally affect the bistable switch.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of state compositions.

claim: Two species competing for the same growth-limiting nutrient cannot coexist with each other according to the competitive exclusion principle.
source: The competitive exclusion principle states that, in general, two species competing for the same growth-limiting nutrient cannot coexist with each other.
evidence: This is a statement of the competitive exclusion principle.

claim: In any state of the model, every species has a unique nutrient limiting its growth.
source: Note that in any state of our model every species has a unique nutrient limiting its growth.
evidence: This follows from Liebig's law as applied in the model.

claim: If a nutrient is limiting the growth of any species at all, such species is also unique.
source: By the virtue of the Rule 1, if a nutrient is limiting the growth of any species at all, such species is also unique.
evidence: This follows from the competitive exclusion principle.

claim: The number of species present in a steady state of the community cannot exceed the total number of nutrients they consume.
source: Just like in the MacArthur model (MacArthur and Levins, 1964) or any other consumer-resource model for that matter, the number of species present in a steady state of the community cannot exceed the total number of nutrients they consume.
evidence: This is a general principle of consumer-resource models.
